title: In the seen, only the seen
hookLine: to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard

lines: YOU'RE NOT EVEN ON THE WAY.
HE FOLLOWS HIM INTO THE STREET.
cards: On the coast at Supparaka lives a man called Bahiya of the bark cloth, because he dresses in strips of bark. People honor him and bring him food and robes; many think he's fully awakened. One day he wonders it himself.
And a deity who wishes him well, the text says, tells him plainly: you're not, and you're not even on the way. But in Savatthi, far to the north, there's someone who is.
Bahiya sets out at once; the text says he never stayed more than one night anywhere on the way. At the monastery he's told the Teacher has gone into town for alms. So he follows him into the street.

teach.b: Bahiya finds the Buddha walking for alms, falls at his feet, and asks: teach me. It's not the time, the Buddha says; we've come into town for alms.
Bahiya asks again, and gives his reason: life is uncertain, yours and mine. Not the time, the Buddha says again. A third time Bahiya asks.

teach.h: IN THE STREET, WITH THE BOWL.
teach.b: And there in the street, alms bowl in hand, the Buddha gives him a teaching only a few lines long. Train yourself like this, Bahiya.
In the seen, there will be only the seen. In the heard, only the heard. In the sensed, only the sensed.
In the known, only the known. When that's so, you won't be with it. When you're not with it, you won't be in it.
Then you'll be neither here nor beyond nor in between. That is the end of suffering. Look at the first line.
You see a face in a crowd, and instantly the mind adds: she's frowning at me, I must have done something, I always do this. The seen was a face. Everything else was added.
The teaching asks Bahiya to stop at the face: not to stop seeing, but to stop building on top of it.

teach.h: NOTHING ADDED, NO ONE IN THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: When nothing is added, there's no I standing in the middle, taking it personally.

teach.h: IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.
teach.b: Then the Buddha walks on with his bowl.

how: Meditation teachers in Theravada and other traditions often give the Bahiya instruction as a practice of bare attention: noting what is seen, heard, sensed and known, without adding to it.

o: a vision sent by a deity in a dream
the seen: just what meets the eye
a secret vision kept for a chosen few

games.q: in the seen: tap the pairs.
p: you're not even on the way

s: the Buddha taught Bahiya the first time he asked
he said it wasn't the time; Bahiya asked three times.
Bahiya's reason was that life is uncertain
he said both his life and the Buddha's were uncertain.
'only the seen' means stop looking at things
it means see, and stop adding stories on top of what's seen.

games.q: you're Bahiya. you've traveled far to find the Teacher, and he says, it's not the time, we're on alms round. what do you do?
o: wait at the monastery until evening.
ask again, because life is uncertain.
games.why: he asks three times. on the third, the Buddha teaches him right there in the street: in the seen, only the seen.

practice: Rest your open eyes on something near you, a cup, a patch of wall, and let it be only what's seen: color, shape, light. When the mind adds a name, a story or an opinion, notice that it's added and come back.
Then close your eyes and do the same with sound, letting a passing car be just a rising and falling sound.

wordCard.voice: Dittha, the seen. The Buddha's teaching to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; nothing added, and no one in the middle.

orig.note: Pali dittha: the seen. 'dittha ditthamattam': in the seen, only the seen.

carryVoice: Your line: stop at the face. The rest of the story can wait. More of Bahiya tomorrow.
